claim: Anatomical studies in diverse species highlight that the insula is one of the most complex anatomical hubs in the mammalian brain.

claim: There is no comprehensive connectivity map of the IC of the mouse.

claim: The mouse IC was divided into three equally large subregions along its rostro-caudal extent: anterior, medial, and posterior insular parts (aIC, mIC, and pIC).
source: Toward the goal of providing a connectivity-based structure to future functional studies, we divided the mouse IC into three equally large subregions along its rostro-caudal extent, namely an anterior, medial, and posterior insular part (aIC, mIC, and pIC, respectively) spanning its entire extent.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Connectivity differences between granular (GI), dysgranular (DI) or agranular (AI) parts of the IC have been reported previously.
source: Although connectivity differences between granular (GI), dysgranular (DI) or agranular (AI) parts of the IC have been reported previously (Maffei et al., 2012), we did not distinguish them here, due to the technical challenge of specifically targeting these subdivisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The study did not distinguish between granular (GI), dysgranular (DI) or agranular (AI) parts of the IC due to the technical challenge of specifically targeting these subdivisions.

claim: Modified SAD∆G-eGFP(EnvA) rabies virus has been shown to label monosynaptic inputs to selected starter cells with high specificity.
source: In order to trace the monosynaptic inputs to the IC, we utilized a modified SAD∆G-eGFP(EnvA) rabies virus (RV), which has been shown to label monosynaptic inputs to selected starter cells with high specificity (Wall et al., 2010; Wickersham et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The modified rabies virus lacks the genes coding for the rabies virus glycoprotein (G) and is pseudotyped with the avian viral envelope EnvA.
source: This virus lacks the genes coding for the rabies virus glycoprotein (G) and is pseudotyped with the avian viral envelope EnvA.
evidence: This describes the technical characteristics of the virus used.

claim: The modified rabies virus infection is restricted to neurons expressing the avian TVA receptor and to monosynaptic retrograde infection of afferents.
source: This restricts its infection to neurons expressing the avian TVA receptor and to monosynaptic retrograde infection of afferents (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the viral tracing system, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The IC of Camk2a-Cre and Gad2-Cre expressing mouse lines were infected to specifically target TVA and rabies virus glycoprotein expression to excitatory pyramidal or inhibitory interneurons, respectively.
source: We infected the IC of Camk2a-Cre and Gad2-Cre expressing mouse lines to specifically target TVA and rabies virus glycoprotein expression to excitatory pyramidal or inhibitory interneurons, respectively (see Figure 1A and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for cell-type-specific tracing.

claim: Cre-dependent adenoassociated virus (AAV2/5-DIO-eYFP) was injected into Camk2a-Cre and Gad2-Cre transgenic mice to trace and quantify axonal projections (outputs) of the IC.
source: In order to trace and quantify the axonal projections (outputs) of the IC, we injected Cre-dependent adenoassociated virus (AAV2/5-DIO-eYFP) into Camk2a-Cre and Gad2-Cre transgenic mice (see Figure 1B and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for output tracing.

claim: Long-range projections from IC Gad2-Cre tracings were not observed.
source: We did not observe long-range projections from IC Gad2-Cre tracings (data not shown).

claim: Only outputs from excitatory projection neurons performed in Camk2a-Cre transgenic mice are presented for IC outputs.
source: Therefore, we here only present outputs from excitatory projection neurons performed in Camk2a-Cre transgenic mice.
evidence: This describes the scope of the output data presented.

source: In some cases, a small percentage of starter neurons were detected in regions outside the boundaries of the IC, including in the Pir, S1 and S2, as well as the M1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C).

evidence: This is a result from the analysis of spillover effects.

claim: Brains where separate starter cell populations were detected outside the IC were excluded.
source: However, we excluded brains where separate starter cell populations were detected outside the IC (see example picture Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, right) or that did not yield strong starter cell populations (see also Materials and methods for exclusion criteria).

claim: In WT mice lacking Cre-recombinase, only some GFP+ neurons were detected at the injection sites within the boundaries that would normally be excluded from quantitative analysis.
source: Mice lacking Cre-recombinase should not express eGFP when infected with RV. Indeed only some GFP+ neurons were detected at the injection sites within the boundaries that we would normally exclude from our quantitative analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the control experiments.

claim: In TVA control conditions (TVA and RV without RG), eGFP expression was detected in transfected neurons, but none was expressed outside the boundaries that would normally be excluded from quantitative analysis.
source: To test the dependence on RG supplementation for the synaptic jump of the virus and thus to ensure the monosynaptic restriction, we injected TVA and RV into Camk2a-Cre or Gad2-Cre mice without the addition of RG. As expected, eGFP expression was detected in transfected neurons, but none was expressed outside the boundaries that we would normally exclude from our quantitative analysis, indicating that no synaptic jump had occurred and no long-range projections were labeled (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the control experiments confirming monosynaptic restriction.

claim: The control experiments indicate that no synaptic jump had occurred and no long-range projections were labeled in the absence of RG.
source: As expected, eGFP expression was detected in transfected neurons, but none was expressed outside the boundaries that we would normally exclude from our quantitative analysis, indicating that no synaptic jump had occurred and no long-range projections were labeled (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control experiment results.

source: To provide a detailed account of the brain-wide connectivity of the mouse IC, we analyzed its bidirectional connectivity with 75 anatomical subregions (the detailed connectivity maps of the IC with all subregions analyzed can be found in the Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).

source: In both cases, posthoc testing showed that this difference was due to stronger inputs to the aIC compared with both other IC subregions for both the excitatory (aIC vs. mIC **p=0.0082, aIC vs. pIC **p=0.0059) and the inhibitory inputs (aIC vs. mIC and aIC vs. pIC **p=0.0031) (Figure 5C).

claim: The aIC strongly and densely innervated the VM, MD and CM.

claim: There was a significant correlation for the connectivity of the mIC and pIC with other cortical regions.
source: We first assessed the reciprocity of the connections between the IC and other cortical regions. We found a significant correlation for the connectivity of the mIC and pIC with other cortical regions and a strong trend for correlation for the mIC with other cortical regions.

claim: No region strongly reversed its connectivity characteristic when comparing between aIC, mIC and pIC.
source: No region strongly reversed its connectivity characteristic when comparing between aIC, mIC and pIC.

claim: The CeA was strongly innervated by the IC without sending backward projections.

evidence: This is a result from the reciprocity analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The striatum, midbrain and hindbrain connectivity was mostly dominated by projections from the IC to the subcortical regions.
source: Interestingly, the thalamus was mostly bidirectionally connected with the IC, whereas the striatum, midbrain and hindbrain connectivity was mostly dominated by projections from the IC to the subcortical regions (Figure 6B, bottom).
evidence: This is a result from the reciprocity analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a high degree of similarity for the input-input comparisons (average correlation coefficients of 0.7 ± 0.16).
source: Overall, there was a high degree of similarity for the input-input comparisons (average correlation coefficients of 0.7 ± 0.16), and, to a lesser extent, for the output-output comparison (average correlation coefficients of 0.45 ± 0.28).

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the correlation analysis.

evidence: This is a result from the hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: The input- and output-patterns of aIC suggest a functional difference compared to mIC and pIC regions.
source: Taken together, the input- and output-patterns of aIC suggest a functional difference compared to mIC and pIC regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering analysis.

source: In particular, for the output network, a key difference arises from the high degree of efferent connectivity between the aIC and striatum, and to a lesser extent, the motor cortex, as compared with the mIC and pIC (Figure 2A).

claim: All IC subregions exhibit multifaceted and brain-wide connectivity patterns, with a substantial degree of intra-insular cross talk.
source: All IC subregions exhibit multifaceted and brain-wide connectivity patterns, with a substantial degree of intra-insular cross talk.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the connectivity data.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multifaceted connectivity patterns observed.

source: By performing unbiased cluster analysis, we found differences in IC connectivity along the rostral-caudal axis, in particular in regards to both in- and outputs to and from the aIC as compared to those of the mIC and pIC.

source: For the outputs, this difference is in part due to a specifically strong ventro-lateral striatum innervation by the aIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connectivity data.

claim: The aIC showed a bias toward connectivity with locomotion-related areas, such as the motor cortices (M1, and M2), the ventro-medial (VM) and centro-median thalamic (CM) nuclei and, the substantia nigra and the midbrain reticular nucleus.
source: Overall, the aIC also showed a bias toward connectivity with locomotion-related areas, such as the motor cortices (M1, and M2), the ventro-medial (VM) and centro-median thalamic (CM) nuclei and, the substantia nigra and the midbrain reticular nucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connectivity data.

claim: This connectivity pattern may provide an anatomical foundation for why optogenetic stimulation of the aIC can elicit appetitive and seeking behavior and has been described as a 'positive valence' region.
source: This connectivity pattern may provide an anatomical foundation for why optogenetic stimulation of the aIC can elicit appetitive and seeking behavior and has been described as a 'positive valence' region (Peng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the connectivity data to previous functional studies.

claim: The data suggest a general role of the aIC with functional roles beyond that of a 'sweet cortical field'.
source: Overall, our data suggest a general role of the aIC with functional roles beyond that of a 'sweet cortical field' (Peng et al., 2015), since intra-insular projections from the mIC and pIC, which process diverse bodily information, are one of its main input sources.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity data in the context of previous functional studies.

claim: Based on its connectivity and knowledge gained in previous functional studies, the aIC could serve as an integrator of positive-valence signals that then guide motivated behavior through its downstream projections, in particular via the ventral striatum and motor cortex.
source: Based on its connectivity and knowledge gained in previous functional studies, the aIC could serve as an integrator of positive-valence signals that then guide motivated behavior through its downstream projections, in particular via the ventral striatum and motor cortex.

claim: Studies performed in hamsters and rats have suggested a further distinction of projection patterns between the AID and AIV.
source: Given our approach we could not dissect further differences between the dorsal (AID) and ventral division of aIC (AIV), but studies performed in hamsters and rats have suggested a further distinction of projection patterns between the AID and AIV (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Maffei et al., 2012; McDonald et al., 1999; Reep and Winans, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in other species.

claim: The correlation and clustering analysis suggests that the mIC is more similar to the pIC.
source: Interestingly, our correlation and clustering analysis suggests that the mIC is more similar to the pIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation and clustering analysis.

claim: The GI/DI of the mIC is referred to as the 'gustatory cortex' in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas.
source: The GI/DI of the mIC is referred to as the 'gustatory cortex' in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas.

source: Notably, we found that the mIC received strong olfactory related inputs (from the Pir, APir, and piriform-amygdalar area (CxA)).
evidence: This is a result from the connectivity analysis.

source: Furthermore, compared to the aIC and pIC, the mIC sends more outputs to memory related areas, such as the entorhinal cortex and the ventral hippocampus.
evidence: This is a result from the connectivity analysis.

source: Indeed, previous studies demonstrated the role of the mIC in conditioned taste aversion (CTA) (Lavi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

source: Taken together with previous functional studies, our anatomical description supports a role for the mIC as a learning hub, involved in various aspects of consummatory behaviors, such as texture processing of food, palatability, taste aversion or preference.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mIC function based on connectivity and previous studies.

claim: The mIC role could extend past consummatory domains, into social transmission of food preferences or reproductive behavior.
source: Potentially, this could extend past consummatory domains, into social transmission of food preferences or reproductive behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the mIC function.

claim: The pIC exhibits a multimodal convergence of inputs from subcortical sites carrying bodily and limbic information streams.
source: The pIC exhibits a multimodal convergence of inputs from subcortical sites carrying bodily and limbic information streams.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The pIC sends strong projections to subcortical regions implicated in emotional and motivated functions.
source: In addition, it sends strong projections to subcortical regions implicated in emotional and motivated functions (Simmons et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connectivity analysis, with a citation to previous work.

claim: The pIC innervates sensory, autonomic, motor associative and limbic structures.
source: This includes innervation of sensory, autonomic, motor associative and limbic structures.
evidence: This is a result from the connectivity analysis.

claim: There are more intra-insular outputs from the pIC than from the aIC, implying a caudal-to-rostral flow of information.
source: Furthermore, there are more intra-insular outputs from the pIC than from the aIC, implying a caudal-to-rostral flow of information, as has been suggested previously (Craig, 2009; Fujita et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the connectivity analysis, consistent with previous suggestions.

claim: The analysis of the reciprocity of IC connectivity with other cortical or subcortical regions revealed strong correlations between in- and outputs for cortical regions across all IC subregions.
source: Our analysis of the reciprocity of IC connectivity with other cortical or subcortical regions revealed strong correlations between in- and outputs for cortical regions across all IC subregions.
evidence: This is a result from the reciprocity analysis.

claim: Many subcortical regions sent strong projections to the IC (raphe nuclei (RN), basal forebrain (BF), olfactory regions, and thalamic nuclei) or predominantly received axonal inputs from the IC (CeA, striatum, SNr, and BNST), revealing strong directionality of connections between the IC and subcortical regions.
source: In contrast, many subcortical regions sent strong projections to the IC (raphe nuclei (RN), basal forebrain (BF), olfactory regions, and thalamic nuclei) or predominantly received axonal inputs from the IC (CeA, striatum, SNr, and BNST), revealing strong directionality of connections between the IC and subcortical regions.
evidence: This is a result from the reciprocity analysis.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons, irrespective of which IC subregion was analyzed (APir aside), displayed very similar connectivity patterns and strength when compared to excitatory pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, inhibitory interneurons, irrespective of which IC subregion was analyzed (APir aside), displayed very similar connectivity patterns and strength when compared to excitatory pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connectivity comparison.

claim: The similar connectivity patterns of inhibitory and excitatory neurons is in agreement with several rabies virus tracings studies in other brain regions.
source: This was supported by our correlation and hierarchical cluster analysis and is in agreement with several rabies virus tracings studies in other brain regions (Beier et al., 2015; Do et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2019; Wall et al., 2016) and may underlie the balance of excitation and inhibition in cortex (Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011).

claim: The similar connectivity patterns of inhibitory and excitatory neurons may underlie the balance of excitation and inhibition in cortex.
source: This was supported by our correlation and hierarchical cluster analysis and is in agreement with several rabies virus tracings studies in other brain regions (Beier et al., 2015; Do et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2019; Wall et al., 2016) and may underlie the balance of excitation and inhibition in cortex (Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

source: Contamination into ventrally or dorsally neighboring non-IC regions may also influence the results we observed.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study.

source: We did not find that tracings with more spillover would systematically exhibit more connectivity to other regions of the brain compared to the same tracing with less spillover, confirming that the amount of spillover did not qualitatively bias our results (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the spillover analysis.

claim: There was a sizable amount of spillover into Pir specifically for the input tracings to the excitatory neurons of the aIC.
source: However, while spillover was very limited for most tracing conditions, there was a sizable amount of spillover into Pir specifically for the input tracings to the excitatory neurons of the aIC.
evidence: This describes a specific limitation of the aIC excitatory input tracings.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

source: Taken together, while it is important to note that our aIC rabies tracings onto excitatory neurons contain a sizeable amount of Pir starter cells, based on the nature of differences we observed between aIC and mIC/pIC connectivity as well as existing Pir tracing results, we do not believe that this spillover affects the main conclusions on aIC versus mIC/pIC connectivity we make in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the impact of the Pir spillover limitation.

claim: Injection sites were aimed toward the center of the IC to limit spillover into the neighboring motor and somatosensory cortices.
source: In order to limit spillover into the neighboring motor and somatosensory cortices, injection sites were aimed toward the center of the IC.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to minimize spillover.

source: As AAV tracing originating from three different starter locations and differing sizes of starter cell populations led to varying degrees of axonal labeling, acquisition settings had to be adjusted for each brain individually.
